newsitem.title: UK: Shell invites bids for Fulmar buoy disposal.
newsitem.headline: Shell invites bids for Fulmar buoy disposal.

text.p: Shell U.K. Exploration and Production (Shell Expro) said on Monday it was inviting bids for decommissioning a 5,000-tonne mooring buoy in use until 1994 on the North Sea Fulmar export system.

The buoy, currently at anchor in a deepwater Norwegian fjord northeast of Stavanger, provided secure anchorage for a converted tanker which acted as a floating storage unit (FSU) for crude oil from the Fulmar, Auk, Clyde and Gannet fields.

Shell Expro, which operates in the North Sea on behalf of Royal Dutch/Shell Group and Exxon Corp, said it had identified onshore disposal as its best environmental option but was open to suggestions for reuse.
"Of course a lot depends on the response we get, but the preferred route would be for it to be taken onshore for scrapping," said an official.
A notice will be placed shortly in the Official Journal of the European Communities and a final decision would be taken in a "couple of months", the official said.
Two 16-inch diameter oil production lines which run through the buoy were flushed clean when it was removed from the fields in the summer of 1994.
This disposal would be much more straightforward than decommissioning Brent Spar, mainly due to the size of the buoy, the official said.
"It's a much smaller structure. This one's easy," said a spokesman.
Nearly two years ago, Shell was forced to abandon plans to ditch the obsolete Brent Spar oil storage buoy in the Atlantic after a high profile campaign by environmentalists.
Independent experts are currently examining the technical, safety and environmental aspects of 11 shortlisted proposals for re-using or scrapping the installation.

Last December, Shell Expro sold the Fulmar FSU to Norway's Smedvig and Statoil for about $5 million. The vessel will be marketed as a floating production unit for projects in the Far East and West Africa.

Crude oil from the Fulmar system is currently being exported via a leased tanker loading system, which will stay in place until a new pipeline linking the fields to the Phillips-operated system is fully commissioned.
